items.prompt: What is the real test for whether code has a single responsibility?
choices: It is written as a single function with no helper calls
Only one kind of change would ever require editing it
It has just one loop
items.explanation: The test is about reasons to change, not size or syntax.

items.prompt: A function has five literal steps that all serve one purpose and change together. How many responsibilities does it have?
choices: Five
Two
One
items.explanation: Steps are not responsibilities. One purpose that changes as a unit is one responsibility.

items.prompt: Which pair counts as two different reasons to change a report method?
choices: A pricing update and a logo redesign
Fixing a typo and then fixing a second typo in a comment
Two developers reading the same lines in the same file
items.explanation: Pricing and branding come from different concerns and owners, so they change independently.

items.prompt: In the opening incident, why was billing at risk during a rebrand?
choices: Billing is always more fragile than layout, so it breaks first
The designer asked for rate edits
Billing lines shared a method with the layout lines
items.explanation: The layout request required editing a method that also held billing, so billing was reachable by accident.

items.prompt: Does being ten lines long guarantee a single responsibility?
choices: No, two lines could answer to different owners
Yes, because code that short cannot mix concerns
Yes, provided that it contains no comments at all
items.explanation: Size says nothing about how many kinds of change would touch the code.

items.prompt: Compared with 'one reason to change', what does 'does one thing' mostly describe?
choices: How the code will change later
How the code reads now, not how it will change
How fast the code runs
items.explanation: It is an impression of the present. Reasons to change look forward.

items.prompt: Three unrelated requests all need edits inside one method. What does that signal?
choices: The requests were badly timed and should be merged into one
The method carries three responsibilities
The method is slow
items.explanation: Each unrelated request is a separate reason to change, so three reasons mean three responsibilities.

items.prompt: Which statement about step count is correct?
choices: Two steps can still be one responsibility
Two steps always mean two separate responsibilities
Step count is the SRP test
items.explanation: If both steps serve one purpose and change together, they are one responsibility.

items.prompt: A 10-line `sendWelcomeEmail(user)` builds the subject and body text, then calls the mail provider with a retry policy. Marketing edits the wording; operations edits the retries. What is the verdict?
choices: One responsibility, because it all serves sending one email
One responsibility, because ten lines is under any sensible limit
Two reasons to change, so two responsibilities despite only ten lines
Undecidable, since the test applies only to whole classes, not to functions
items.explanation: Wording and retry policy come from different owners on different schedules. Short length and a shared goal do not make them one reason.
items.reference:
Two ways to read 'does one thing'
looks one-purpose now: reads as a single story
one reason to change: only one kind of request edits it
generate(): rebrand + pricing + new data source = 3 reasons
Why: the test predicts what will force edits, not how the code reads today.
items.learnMore:
Reasons to change

Ask who could request an edit to this code and why. If the requests come from unrelated concerns or owners, the code carries more than one responsibility, however short it is.

Common mistake

Counting lines or literal steps. A short function can mix concerns and a long one can serve a single purpose.
items.reflection: Think of a document, spreadsheet or routine you maintain. List the different people or events that could force you to edit it. Does the count surprise you?

items.prompt: Function A has twelve steps that all apply one shipping-rate table. Function B has three lines: it parses a date and writes an audit log entry. Which is more likely to violate single responsibility?
choices: B, since parsing and audit logging have different owners
A, because twelve steps exceed what any single function should hold
Neither, because both are short enough to read in a single pass
A, because longer functions change more often than shorter ones
items.explanation: A has one reason to change (the rate table). B mixes two concerns. Length is not the test.

Run it with sample input and confirm it returns a single value
List who could ask for an edit and see if the answers differ

items.prompt: Is there one universally correct place to draw a responsibility boundary?
choices: Yes, one boundary after every function, no matter what
Yes, the boundary belongs at every ten lines of code, in every codebase
No, it depends on what changes independently in this codebase
items.explanation: Boundaries follow real change patterns, which differ between codebases.

items.prompt: One developer owns both validation rules and their error wording and always changes them together. Should they be split?
choices: Probably not, because they share one reason to change
Yes, always, because rules and wording are different words
Yes, into three separate files, one per kind of message
items.explanation: Changes that always move together are one reason to change.

items.prompt: Compliance owns the rules and a writer owns the wording, on different schedules. Should they be split?
choices: No, same function is always fine
No, wording is never a separate concern
Yes, because they have different owners and schedules
items.explanation: Independent owners and schedules make these two reasons to change.

items.prompt: Which input to the SRP judgment is about people rather than code?
choices: Who asks for each kind of change, and how often
The number of characters allowed on each line
Which programming language the team is currently using
items.explanation: Reasons to change come from people and processes, so ownership matters.

items.prompt: Why can the same code be right in one system and wrong in another?
choices: Programming languages differ in what counts as a function boundary
The changes may be independent in one and linked in the other
Compilers treat boundaries differently depending on the build settings
items.explanation: The code is the same. The surrounding change patterns are not.

items.prompt: SRP is best described as which of these?
choices: A fixed rule with a single universal answer
A judgment informed by context
A matter of taste
items.explanation: It has a clear test but the answer depends on the codebase.

items.prompt: Two parts of a function always change in the same commit by the same person. How many reasons to change do they have?
choices: One
Two
Zero
items.explanation: They move together, so they behave as one reason.

items.prompt: Which fact most helps decide where a boundary belongs?
choices: Which parts have the longest names
Which parts have changed independently before
Which parts were written first by the original team
items.explanation: Past independent changes predict future ones.

items.prompt: In team X one developer sets pricing rates and invoice layout together in every release. In team Y finance owns rates and a brand team owns layout. The code is identical. Which statement is most defensible?
choices: Both teams must split, because the code is identical in both
Neither team may split, since identical code needs identical structure
Only X should split, since a single owner handles both concerns
Splitting is justified in Y, while X may reasonably keep them together
items.explanation: The test depends on how changes arrive. Same code, different owners, different verdicts.
items.reference:
Same code, two contexts
one developer owns rules and wording: one reason, keep together
compliance owns rules, a writer owns wording: two reasons, split
the code is identical in both
Why: the right boundary depends on what changes independently in this codebase.
items.learnMore:
Boundaries depend on context

A boundary belongs where changes are likely to arrive independently: different owners, different schedules, different triggers. Look at who asks for changes and how often they move together.

Common mistake

Treating a boundary that worked in one team as a universal rule for every team.
items.reflection: Pick two things in your own work that sit together today. Who asks for changes to each? Would the answer ever make you pull them apart?

items.prompt: A team splits billing from layout 'because the book says to', yet both always change in one pull request by the same author. What is the strongest critique?
choices: A split only counts as proper SRP when it is made by file
The split has no independent reason to change behind it
Billing should never share a file with anything else, ever
They should have split into even more pieces than they did
items.explanation: A boundary without independent change patterns adds indirection and no benefit.

A teammate's strong preference for smaller files in general
Rule edits and wording edits landing in unrelated pull requests
The function taking exactly two parameters, one for each concern
items.explanation: Evidence of independent change is the direct signal. Length and preference are proxies.

items.prompt: What is the first step of the decision procedure?
choices: List every distinct reason the code might change
Count the lines in the function
Find the deepest nested block in the function body
items.explanation: You need the reasons before you can count them.

items.prompt: Exactly one distinct reason is found. What should you do?
choices: Split it in half
Rewrite it as a class
Nothing, it already has a single responsibility
items.explanation: One reason means the unit is already focused.

items.prompt: More than one distinct reason is found. What does that mean?
choices: A candidate for splitting along those lines
The code is correct as written and should not change
A sign the code needs more comments and documentation
items.explanation: Each distinct reason suggests a separate unit.

items.prompt: In handleSignup, which two parts have different reasons to change?
choices: Reading the request and reading the response
Validation rules and response formatting
Variable naming and indentation
items.explanation: Business rules and envelope shape come from different concerns.

items.prompt: After the split, what is handleSignup's one reason to change?
choices: A password rule changes
The sequence of signup steps changes
The response envelope gets a new API-version field
items.explanation: It now only coordinates the order of steps.

items.prompt: A request arrives to reject signups after too many attempts from one IP. What is it?
choices: A new distinct reason to change
Another form of response formatting
A reason to merge the units back
items.explanation: Abuse policy is separate from validation and formatting.

items.prompt: Are a password-rule change and an envelope-shape change the same reason?
choices: Yes, both are about signup
No, they are different concerns with different owners
Yes, both are about signup, since they ship in one release
items.explanation: Sharing a feature name does not make two changes the same reason.

items.prompt: Does the test stop applying once a function has been split?
choices: Yes, once the split is done
Yes, unless the team grows past a certain size
No, a new kind of change means asking again
items.explanation: Every new kind of change is a new chance for a bundle.

items.prompt: After splitting, a colleague says handleSignup still 'does both things' by calling them. What is the best reply?
choices: Correct, so it should be deleted and callers should invoke both functions directly
It owns only the order of the steps, which changes for its own reason
Correct, so it needs a further split into two separate orchestrator functions
Wrong, because calls to other functions never count toward responsibilities
items.explanation: Orchestration is its own reason to change: the sequence or composition of steps.
items.reference:
The decision procedure
1. list every distinct reason the code might change
2. one reason: leave it
3. more than one: split along those reasons
4. new kind of change later: ask again
Why: the count of independent reasons, not the shape of the code, decides the split.
items.learnMore:
Applying the procedure

In handleSignup, a password rule and an envelope field are different concerns with different owners. After the split, handleSignup keeps one reason: the order of signup steps. A new kind of change, like rate limiting, restarts the question.

Common mistake

Believing that an orchestrating function still has all of its callees' responsibilities. Calling a unit is not owning its logic.
items.reflection: Take a routine you do (cooking, a weekly report, a deploy). If something around it changed, which step would you edit, and which steps would stay untouched?

items.prompt: Rate limiting is added to the split signup flow. Where does it belong?
choices: Inside validateSignup, as one more check on the request
Inside formatSignupResponse, as an extra field in the result envelope
Nowhere, since it is not a reason to change
In a new step such as checkRateLimit that handleSignup coordinates
items.explanation: Abuse policy is a fourth reason to change. Putting it in validateSignup recreates the bundle.

items.prompt: What is the overcorrection in single responsibility?
choices: Keeping every concern together in one very large function
Writing tests for every function before writing the code
Splitting into tiny pieces with no independent reasons
items.explanation: Splitting without independent reasons adds cost and no benefit.

items.prompt: getEmailField only feeds isValidEmailFormat, which only feeds validateEmail. Do they have independent reasons to change?
choices: No, they change together
Yes, one each
Yes, but only once the system has grown large
items.explanation: They exist to implement one check, so they share one reason.

items.prompt: What does over-splitting cost?
choices: Slower execution in every case
More names and jumps to follow, with no benefit
Fewer tests passing
items.explanation: Readers pay a navigation cost for every extra unit.

items.prompt: Is 'can this be split further?' a good SRP question?
choices: Yes, because it shows where the next split goes
No, almost anything can be split further
Yes, whenever the function has over five lines
items.explanation: Splittability is not the test. Independence of change is.

items.prompt: Which question replaces it?
choices: Would splitting let two changes avoid each other's code?
Is the function longer than one screen?
Does the function body contain any loop or branch at all?
items.explanation: A split pays off only if it separates changes.

items.prompt: handleSignup bundled two independent reasons. What did the email chain do?
choices: Bundled two reasons together
Broke one reason into several pieces
Hid a bug in the middle of the long chain
items.explanation: The two mistakes are opposite: too few units versus too many.

items.prompt: Which is evidence that a split was worth it?
choices: There are now more files
Each function is now short enough to read at a glance
Two kinds of change now land in different units
items.explanation: The benefit is independent change, not file count.

items.prompt: Which cost appears every time someone reads over-split code?
choices: Extra jumps between tiny functions
Longer compile times
Louder linter warnings on every build
items.explanation: Following one idea across many tiny units takes effort.

items.prompt: A chain parseAmount, validateAmount, checkPositive has one line each, is called only from validatePayment and is owned by one person. What is the best action?
choices: Split them further so that each line gets its own test file
Keep them as they are, since small functions are always preferred
Merge them back, since they share one reason to change
Move each of them to a separate module for extra isolation
items.explanation: No piece changes independently of the others, so the split adds cost only.
items.reference:
Two opposite mistakes
too few units: handleSignup bundles 2 independent reasons
too many units: getEmailField, isValidEmailFormat, validateEmail share 1 reason
right size: one unit per independent reason
Why: both directions cost something; the test counts reasons, not functions.
items.learnMore:
When not to split

A split earns its place only if it lets two different future changes avoid each other's code. Pieces that only exist to feed each other add names and jumps without that benefit.

Common mistake

Asking 'can this be split further?' Almost anything can. Ask whether the pieces would ever change independently.
items.reflection: Where in your own work have you broken something into so many small parts that the parts were harder to follow than the whole? What would you merge back?

items.prompt: Compare the bundled handleSignup with the three-function email chain. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The first has too few units for its reasons, the second too many
Both have too few units, at different scales of the code
Both have too many units, though at different scales of code
The first is correct as written, and only the second is a mistake
items.explanation: One bundled two independent reasons; the other split a single reason.

items.prompt: What was the root cause of the overbilling incident?
choices: Billing lived inside the method a layout change edited
A typo in a decimal number, and nothing structural behind it
A missing comment above the line that sets the billing rate
items.explanation: The typo triggered it. The structure made billing reachable.

items.prompt: Which of these is a structural fix?
choices: Adding a review checklist item
Moving billing into its own unit
Asking every engineer to be more careful
items.explanation: A structural fix removes the opportunity, not just the chance of missing it.

items.prompt: In a method with three equal responsibilities, what share is unrelated to any one edit?
choices: About one third
About two thirds
About three quarters
items.explanation: Two of the three blocks are unrelated, which is 66.7%.

items.prompt: When only one responsibility is in the method, what share is unrelated?
items.explanation: With nothing else in the method, there is nothing unrelated to hit.

items.prompt: After the split, what does generate() own?
choices: The billing rates
Orchestration: calling the three units in order
The PDF layout, fonts and header images for each report
items.explanation: Its reason to change is the sequence of steps.

items.prompt: An enterprise pricing tier is requested. Which unit changes?
choices: ReportPdfRenderer
UsageDataFetcher
BillingCalculator
items.explanation: The rate lookup lives in the billing calculator.

items.prompt: Does the split make a wrong rate impossible?
choices: No, it makes accidental edits less likely
Yes, it removes all rate bugs
Yes, as long as files stay small
items.explanation: Someone can still edit the calculator wrongly. Separation reduces accidents.

items.prompt: What pairs with the split to protect billing?
choices: A larger style guide
A longer comment above the rate line
A test that pins billing rates
items.explanation: A test catches a wrong rate whichever file it appears in.

items.prompt: One team adds a review checklist item about billing lines. Another moves billing into its own unit. What is the best description of the difference?
choices: Both remove the risk equally, so either one of them is enough
The checklist removes the risk, and the split only improves readability
The split depends on reviewers noticing, while the checklist changes which code a layout edit can reach
The checklist adds a chance to catch it; the split removes billing from the layout diff
items.explanation: A checklist depends on a reviewer noticing. The split changes which code a layout edit can reach.
items.reference:
Process fix vs structural fix
checklist: a chance to catch the stray edit
split: billing is not in the layout diff at all
3 bundled: 10 of 15 lines unrelated (66.7%)
1 bundled: 0 unrelated lines
Why: removing the reachability of billing from layout work beats relying on attention.
items.learnMore:
What the split changes

After the split a rebrand edits only the renderer, an enterprise tier edits only the billing calculator, and a new usage schema edits only the fetcher. A dedicated rate test protects billing even if someone edits it.

Common mistake

items.prompt: Implement `sumQuantities(events)`: the sum of `quantity` across all events. An empty list gives 0.
items.explanation: reduce adds each quantity to a running total that starts at 0, so an empty list gives 0.

items.prompt: Implement `apiCallCount(events)`: the sum of `quantity` for events whose `type` is `"api_call"`.
items.explanation: Filtering first keeps only the matching events, then the quantities are summed.

items.prompt: Implement `centsFor(event)`: an `api_call` costs 2 cents per unit and `storage` costs 5 cents per unit. Return the cost of one event.
items.explanation: The rates live in one table, and the cost is quantity times the rate for that type.

items.prompt: Implement `totalCents(events)`: the total cost in cents, with `api_call` at 2 and `storage` at 5 cents per unit.
items.explanation: Sum quantity times rate over all events: 10 * 2 + 4 * 5 = 40.

items.prompt: Implement `rateFor(type, tier)`: standard tier rates are api_call 2 and storage 5; the `"enterprise"` tier is api_call 1 and storage 4. Any tier other than `"enterprise"` is standard.
items.explanation: Choose the row for the tier, then look up the event type in it.

items.prompt: Implement `apiCents(events, tier)`: the cost of only the `api_call` events, at 2 cents per unit, or 1 cent per unit when `tier` is `"enterprise"`.
items.explanation: Only the rate depends on the tier. The filtering and summing are unchanged.

items.prompt: Implement `quantityByType(events)`: return `{ api_call: n, storage: m }` with the total quantity for each type (0 when absent). Keep the keys in that order.

tests.expr: expect(quantityByType([{ type: "api_call", quantity: 10 }, { type: "storage", quantity: 4 }])).toEqual({ api_call: 10, storage: 4 })

items.explanation: Start both totals at 0 so absent types report 0, then add each event to its type.

items.prompt: Implement `applyMinimum(total, minimum)`: return `minimum` when `total` is below it, otherwise `total`.
items.explanation: The comparison picks whichever is larger of the total and the floor.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateTotal(usageEvents, tier)` in whole cents. Standard tier: `api_call` 2, `storage` 5 per unit. `"enterprise"` tier: `api_call` 1, `storage` 4 per unit. Any other tier is standard. An empty list gives 0.
items.explanation: The tier only selects a rate table. The multiplication and sum are the same for every tier, so adding a tier adds a row. Enterprise: 10 * 1 + 4 * 4 = 26.
items.reference:
A change that fits in one unit
rates: whole cents per unit (no floating point)
new tier = new row in the rate table
fetcher and renderer never see tiers
Why: when the boundary is right, the whole change is one small function.
items.learnMore:
Extending the calculator

Keep the rates in one table keyed by tier and event type, and have the calculator multiply quantity by the looked-up rate. A new tier then only adds a row.

Common mistake

Hard-coding each tier as its own branch of arithmetic, which spreads rate knowledge across the function.
